name: Knee Collateral and Posterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries
summary: Ligament sprains are graded: grade I (stretch, no laxity), grade II (partial tear, some laxity with a firm end point), grade III (complete tear, laxity without a firm end point). Most isolated MCL injuries heal well with conservative management.

looksLike: MCL: medial knee pain, swelling localised medially, pain with twisting.
PCL: posterior knee pain, mild swelling, difficulty with stairs and deceleration.
Ask: mechanism, pop, ability to continue playing, immediate swelling (haemarthrosis suggests ACL or fracture), locking, giving way, numbness in the foot (peroneal nerve with lateral injuries).
redFlags: Laxity of several ligaments, high-energy trauma
Calf swelling and pain during rehabilitation
firstSteps: Typical return to sport: grade I MCL a few weeks; grade II longer; grade III and PCL longer still. Base return on criteria, not time alone.

mistakes: In PCL injury, the tibia already sags backward at rest. A careless anterior drawer then shows "excessive forward movement" because you start from a sagged position, falsely suggesting an ACL tear. Always look for the sag first.

blocks.text: Ligament sprains are graded: grade I (stretch, no laxity), grade II (partial tear, some laxity with a firm end point), grade III (complete tear, laxity without a firm end point). Most isolated MCL injuries heal well with conservative management [Ref – to verify]. Isolated PCL injuries are often managed conservatively; combined injuries frequently need surgery.

sections.title: B to C. Presentation and questions

items: MCL: medial knee pain, swelling localised medially, pain with twisting.
PCL: posterior knee pain, mild swelling, difficulty with stairs and deceleration.
Ask: mechanism, pop, ability to continue playing, immediate swelling (haemarthrosis suggests ACL or fracture), locking, giving way, numbness in the foot (peroneal nerve with lateral injuries).

blocks.text: Effusion, palpation along the ligaments, range, Ottawa knee rule if acute trauma, ligament stress tests, meniscal screen, neurovascular check (dorsalis pedis pulse, peroneal nerve).

rows: Supine; knee at 0 then 20 to 30 degrees flexion
Stabilise the thigh, push the knee inward with a hand on the lateral knee, other hand pulls the ankle outward
Gapping at 30 degrees: MCL; gapping also at 0 degrees: MCL plus cruciate or capsule involvement
LCL; at 0 degrees suggests combined injury
Supine, hip 45, knee 90 degrees, foot stabilised
Increased posterior translation, soft end feel
Supine, hips and knees at 90 degrees, legs supported at the heels
Tibia sags back compared with the other side
Externally rotate both feet; compare thigh-foot angle
Posterolateral corner (30 only) or PCL plus PLC (30 and 90) [Ref – to verify]

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: In PCL injury, the tibia already sags backward at rest. A careless anterior drawer then shows "excessive forward movement" because you start from a sagged position, falsely suggesting an ACL tear. Always look for the sag first.

rows: Pop, rapid haemarthrosis, giving way, positive Lachman
Ottawa positive, unable to bear weight
Medial knee pain after twisting, apprehension
Multiple ligament laxity, often spontaneously reduced

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Laxity of several ligaments, high-energy trauma
Calf swelling and pain during rehabilitation

steps: **Isolated grade I to II MCL:** functional rehabilitation, early movement.
**Grade III MCL or isolated PCL:** brace and supervised rehabilitation; orthopaedic opinion.
**Multi-ligament or posterolateral corner injury:** surgical referral.

rows: Protect (hinged brace for grade II to III MCL as advised), reduce swelling, quadriceps activation, early range
Quadriceps emphasis, especially for PCL (quadriceps pull the tibia forward). Avoid isolated hamstring curls early in PCL injuries because hamstrings pull the tibia backward
Running, cutting and sport drills once range is full, no effusion, strength near the other side

blocks.text: Typical return to sport: grade I MCL a few weeks; grade II longer; grade III and PCL longer still [Ref – to verify]. Base return on criteria, not time alone.

sections.title: K to M. Modalities and reassessment

blocks.text: Ice and compression early. Measure effusion, range, valgus stress pain, quadriceps strength (limb symmetry), hop tests, IKDC or KOOS.

items: **Why test valgus at 0 and 30 degrees?** Opening at 30 isolates the MCL; opening at 0 indicates additional structures are injured.
**Which muscle group is prioritised in PCL rehab?** Quadriceps.
**What is the sag sign?** Backward sag of the tibia with hips and knees at 90 degrees.
**Why check pulses with multi-ligament laxity?** Knee dislocation can injure the popliteal artery.
**Name a sign of peroneal nerve injury.** Weak ankle dorsiflexion (foot drop) and numbness of the dorsum of the foot.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Perform valgus, varus, posterior drawer, sag and dial tests.
Grade collateral ligament injuries and plan rehabilitation.
Recognise knee dislocation and nerve injury.
